faq: Does this make AI completely safe?

No tool is risk free, and we do not claim that. Rules and filters lower the chance of bad answers, and approval steps put a person in charge of anything important. We tell you plainly what risk remains.
We are not a law firm, so we do not give legal advice. We build common-sense controls and document them, which your lawyer can review against rules that apply to you, such as privacy or industry law.
Can you add this to a tool someone else built?
Yes, if we can edit its instructions or place a filter in front of it. We review how it is built first and tell you what can and cannot be changed.
What about children or sensitive topics?

We can block or redirect topics such as health, money or minors, and set the tool to hand over to a person. We follow the platform rules of the AI provider you use, and help you add an age or disclaimer notice.

desc:
AI safety rules and content filters keep your AI tool on topic, careful with personal data and honest when it is unsure. Ecom Swift LLC writes the rules in plain words, builds them into your tool and tests them with tricky questions before customers see it.

## What are AI safety rules and content filters?

They are the boundaries around an AI tool. Rules say what the tool may do: which topics it covers, which it refuses, how it treats personal data and which actions need a person to approve. Filters enforce those rules by checking what users send in and what the tool sends back.

Together they turn a general-purpose model into a tool with a defined job. A support assistant should talk about orders and returns, not give medical advice or comment on politics.

## Why unguarded tools cause problems

An AI model will try to be helpful with almost any request. Without limits, it may promise refunds you do not offer, repeat private information, follow instructions hidden inside a pasted message or answer questions far outside your business. Some of these failures cost money, and some damage trust.

Written rules also help your staff. When people know what the tool is supposed to do, they can spot when it behaves differently and know who to tell.

## How clear limits improve outcomes

Limits make a tool predictable. Predictable tools are easier to approve, easier to explain to customers and easier to improve, because you can compare behavior against a written standard.

No filter is perfect, and we do not claim otherwise. The aim is to reduce the chance and the impact of mistakes: block what should be blocked, send risky cases to a person and keep a record of what was flagged. The result depends on how the tool is used and on what people try to make it do.

## What a good safety set-up includes

- A one-page rulebook in plain language that staff can read in a few minutes.
- A list of blocked topics and phrases that fit your business.
- A fallback message for questions the tool should not answer.
- Input filters that catch attempts to override its instructions.
- Output filters that check replies before users see them.
- Personal data rules covering what it may ask for, store or repeat.
- Approval steps for actions with real consequences, such as refunds or account changes.
- A named person who receives escalated cases.
- Logging of flagged answers, with notes on what happened.
- A set of tricky test questions you can run again after future changes.

## What we do

We review the tool or its instructions, then write the rulebook with you. We build the filters and approval steps, then test with deliberately awkward questions: off-topic requests, attempts to trick the tool and sensitive situations. We fix what fails and run the tests again.

The Basic package covers one tool with a rulebook, a blocked topics list, a fallback message and a short test set. The Standard package adds input and output filters, approval steps, data handling rules and a larger test set. The Premium package covers more tools, adds logging, escalation to a named person, a guide for staff and moderators, a long test set and a short written risk summary. We can add this to a tool someone else built, if we can read its settings.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Decide what the tool must never do before deciding what it can do.
- Require human approval for anything involving money or accounts.
- Tell users they are talking to an AI tool.
- Keep a route to a real person at every step.
- Re-run the test questions after each change.

**Avoid:**
- Treating a rulebook as a replacement for monitoring.
- Collecting personal data the tool does not need.
- Using a long list of banned words as the only protection.
- Letting the tool give advice in areas such as health or law.
- Assuming a rule works because it is written down.

## Who it is for

A company launching a customer assistant wants clear limits before launch. A store with an existing chatbot has noticed odd replies and wants it tightened. A team building an internal tool wants staff to know what it will and will not do.

## What we need from you

We need to see the tool or its instructions, a description of its audience and any rules you already follow. Share access as a collaborator, team or developer user where the platform allows, and never send passwords. We provide safety design, not legal advice, and we recommend a qualified adviser for regulated areas.
